If it did, the effect's very identity would be the cause's identity and its reality the cause's reality; nothing could then be said of it except what is said of that identity; it would no longer be a distinct existence, and it could not be said to proceed from the cause by being that very cause. Yet though the effect need not share the cause in all its states, it must share it in some; for if it shared it in none, it would not be an effect of it at all, and the cause would not have brought it into existence.

Since this is the way things exist in multiplicity, each must share with its cause in one respect and differ from it in another. It follows, then, that the Follower called Soul — which emanates from the First Intellect, the cause of its existence — must resemble it in one respect and differ from it in another. Since this is so, it is plain that when the Follower called Soul has its existence from the Intellect, its being need not resemble the Intellect in all its states; nor does it follow that what is said of the Intellect as cause must also be said of the Follower called Soul. This refutes what the author of al-Nusra said: that if it were necessary, it would be necessary.

### The Twentieth Section of the First Part

The author of al-Nusra said: This has many parallels in the sensible world, such as thought and the partial soul. For the partial soul that is in us is in the position of the Intellect, and thought is in the position of the Soul. Yet thought, even though it emanates from the soul, may not be said to be like the soul, because thought perceives what it perceives part by part, and time after time, whereas the soul perceives the whole of what it perceives without time. That is his statement.

We say: The soul — I mean the soul of the human being — has acts, and each of its acts has a name proper to it. When it seeks to grasp some thing, that seeking is called thought (al-fikr). When it regards the forms of the known things that have come to be within its essence, that regarding is called retention (al-hifz). When it imprints its essence with the marks it captures by way of inference or by way of the senses, that imprint is called conception (al-tasawwur). And when it knows that outside itself there are things it wishes to conceive, that will is called striving (al-nuzu) toward them.

Since the soul has acts, and thought is an act of it that does not pass beyond its own essence so as to have an existence apart from its existence, how can it be sound to liken thought to the Follower called Soul — which has an existence other than the existence of the Intellect? And how can it be said that thought perceives part by part, when perception belongs only to the essence of the soul, through its act called thought within itself? And how can it be sound that the soul — the soul of the human being — should perceive the whole without time, when its only path to knowledge is through the senses and inference, passing from particulars to universals in time?

Nor does it follow, because thought may not be said to resemble the soul, that the Second Intellect — called the Universal Soul — does not resemble the First Intellect. For thought as it proceeds from human souls does not run in the same course as the Second Intellect from the First Intellect. The Second Intellect is a second existence from origination, subsisting through itself, even though in existence it is one rank below the First. But thought has no existence separate from the soul; rather it is the very identity of the soul, and has no subsistence through itself. Every act of the soul has a cause that makes it necessary: the soul's being in the world of nature. When the soul departs from that world, these acts are annulled with their cause, and nothing remains subsisting except the essence conceived as pure Intellect.

He made the Second Intellect — called the Soul — proceed from the First Intellect in the manner that thought proceeds from the soul. But since the existence of thought is no existence other than the existence of the soul — which he likened to the Intellect — and since thought has no perception of the soul through its own essence, his argument amounts to a denial that the Second Intellect called the Soul has any existence other than the existence of the First Intellect, or any perception like the perception of the First. And that is impossible; for the Follower has an existence other than the existence of the First, and a perception like the perception of the First. It does not deserve to be called an originator, just as the First Existent does not deserve to be called emanated. Both are pure intellects; each has encompassed its own essence and preserved it by its own essence. They are alike in one respect and unlike in another, as the foregoing discussion has established.

Since this is so, there is no sense in the likenings he drew: no sense in making thought stand as what he likened it to, no sense in placing the human soul in the position of the First Intellect, and no sense in placing thought within it in the position of the Universal Soul. For the nobility of the human soul, and its passage from potency to act, lie entirely in acquisition; and acquisition comes only from the senses as deed and from conception as knowledge. Since the nobility of souls lies in acquisition — part of which is thought and inference as conception — and since thought belongs to souls only so that they may be ennobled by it, his argument is as though he had made the cause of the First Intellect's nobility to be the Second Intellect called the Soul. And that is an inverted proposition. For the nobility of the Follower and its rank come from what precedes it in existence — the Antecedent — while the nobility of the Antecedent and its rank come from what comes after it. The rule governing what has a second existence — in respect of perfection and completeness — is that it be the reverse of what has a first existence. Neither, therefore, runs in the course of the other in this respect, though they share from another aspect. Yet the author of al-Nusra has judged what has a first existence by what belongs to what has a second existence. And that is impossible.

chapters.before_md:
**Section One**

The author of al-Islah said:

As for what the author of al-Nusrah has established: we do not say that nature and the dark al-Hayuli (اَلْهَيُولَى) are born from the Second as the Second is born from the First. That world is the world of honor and virtue; this world is the world of darkness and turbidity. The Second, though born from the First, resembles him; the state of al-Hayuli is not like that state.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

This is wrong. Were that world all light with no darkness in it, and this world all darkness with no light in it, no connection would fall between this world and that world. We say rather that the soul has two extremes. One faces the intellect, lying upon its horizon — this is the luminous, noble side. The other faces nature, which lies upon its horizon, and carries some darkness and turbidity, because nature falls upon that horizon. We say likewise that nature has two ends. One faces the partial soul, and in it there is some light, because it falls upon the soul's horizon. The other faces the elements — this is the dark and turbid side, in which there is no light. By these divisions we speak of the soul and of nature, of their darkness and their light. We do not say that that entire world is a world of light with no darkness, nor that this entire world is a world of darkness with no light. Were it as he describes, there would be between them neither neighboring nor pairing.

He said:

It stands established, then, that the dark al-Hayuli is born from the soul, though it does not resemble it, just as the soul is born from the First, though it does not resemble him. Al-Hayuli fell dark by reason of its distance from the First Cause, on account of its being born from the soul. Likewise the diminution fell in the soul, because it is farther from the First Cause — by which I mean the Preceding One (السَّابِق).

This is his statement.

We say:

What the author of al-Islah says in his book is not what the author of al-Nusrah takes it to be. The heart of his argument — his answer to the claim that the Second is born from the First yet does not resemble him — is his own words: we do not say so. We say instead that the Second is born from the First, does not resemble him, yet is his counterpart and likeness, even though the First is higher in rank and nobler in station. This is like the male and the female in all genera and substances: the male, though higher and nobler than the female, is nonetheless the counterpart and likeness of his fellow.

Then we say:

The Second is too noble and elevated for its relation to what lies below it to mirror its relation to the First. The First and the Second are two counterparts, and they are the source of honor, perfection, and elevation — there is no honor above them. God made them the source of perfect honor and perfect light, of complete elevation and complete knowledge, with no ignorance, no turbidity, and no darkness whatsoever. They are the two foundations of the higher world, which is the source of purity, of sanctity (اَلْقُدْس), and of life. Al-Hayuli, by contrast, is a trace of the Second — it is the substance of this world, a turbid and dark substance, not to be described by mercy or by power. The Second manifested it by act out of himself, by the power derived from the First, and then brought forth from it the form, which is nature, by act.

Then the author of al-Islah said:

It is not permissible to say that al-Hayuli is born from him. We say rather that it is a trace of him, and therefore does not resemble him. The Second is born from the First and does resemble him, even though the First is higher in rank.

This is his statement, and its substance is this: the Second issues from the First and is like him, though the First is higher in rank; and al-Hayuli is a trace of the Second, its substance dark and turbid, because the relation of al-Hayuli to the Second is not like the relation of the Second to the First. The First and the Second are counterparts, whereas al-Hayuli does not resemble the Second, being only a trace of him.

If this is the substance of his saying, then what the author of al-Nusrah offers in reply is no reply at all. The author of al-Islah did not assert in his statement that that entire world is light and radiance. He said only, in describing the state of the First and the Second, that God Most High made them the source of honor and elevation. This says nothing about whether things unlike them in state can exist. What has already been offered to indicate that al-Hayuli is not born from the Second is sufficient; there is no need to extend the discussion in ways that might cast suspicion upon an aim we do not hold in this section.

We say:

Al-Hayuli does not resemble the Second, nor the First, because its existence, in its issuing from the First, is by the lower relation that we set forth in our earlier words and in our book known as Rahat al-Aql. In that is sufficiency.

**Section Two of the Third Chapter**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

This statement is wrong, because were that world all light with no darkness in it, and this world all darkness with no light in it, no connection would fall between this world and that world.

We say:

This statement, insofar as it charges the author of al-Islah with something he did not say, is an error; but insofar as it expresses his own view, it is sound. For in the world of origination and issuance there is that which is shared: it suits what is above it by being issued, and it suits what is below it by being a body. It possesses two aspects — it does not resemble the First from whom its existence comes; it resembles the Second in one respect and differs from him in another. The respect in which it resembles him is its being issued from him. The respect in which it resembles the body is its being a natural body. And that is nature. When it is joined to the world of origination and issuance, it is a life flowing from that world into what is below it, giving it what it is able to receive of succession and of conception. When it is joined to this world, it is a principle of motion and stillness in the thing it is in essentially, not by way of accident. So nature came to be, even though in its existence it is issued — an intermediary between the two issuings, the First and the Second.

**Section Three of the Third Chapter**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

The soul — by which I mean the Second — has two extremes. One of them is toward the intellect, upon its horizon, and it is the luminous, noble side. The other is toward nature, upon its horizon, and it is the side in which there is some darkness.

We say:

That is not sound. Whatever has extremes has dimensions measurable by area. The Second — which he has called a soul in the way we have set forth — is not a body, and if it is not a body, it cannot have two extremes. By his words, moreover, he requires the Second to have a luminous extreme upon the horizon of the intellect, and an extreme carrying some darkness upon the horizon of nature — making it distinct from the intellect and distinct from the First by virtue of being upon the horizon of nature. Yet it is impossible that the Second should have any attribute by which it is distinct from the First, since its existence, in its issuing, derives from the nobler relation in the First — namely the First's being a cause. We have already established that the First, in its own essence, is not simultaneously cause and effect. It is cause by relation to what lies below it — this is the nobler relation in the First — and effect by relation to itself, which is the lower relation in the First. From its intellection of its own essence as cause there issues from it its like, for it is the nature of a cause to produce its effect from itself. From its intellection of its essence as effect there issues from it what is not its like, since this issuance derives from the lower relation in the First, namely its being an effect.

What we have said is confirmed by the condition of the Foundation (al-Asas), who is the living likeness of the Second in the knowledge of the body, and who is not distinct from the Speaker (al-Natiq). Everything that exists in the Foundation exists in the Speaker from whom the Foundation's existence comes, and thus the Foundation is not distinct from him. Yet not everything belonging to the Speaker exists in the Foundation, for the Speaker possesses something from which the Foundation is excluded — something the Foundation does not share. It is thus clear that the Foundation is not distinct from the Speaker: it shares with him everything that exists in it, and there is nothing in it that is not also in the Speaker. Since the Foundation is not distinct from the Speaker, and since it is the likeness through which — and through whose rank — the existence and rank of the Second are inferred, the Second is not distinct from the First. And since it is not distinct, its existence as he describes it — upon the horizon of nature — is impossible.

**Section Four of the Third Chapter**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Al-Hayuli fell dark only by reason of its distance from the First Cause, on account of its being born from the soul.

We say:

The unlikeness of al-Hayuli to the First, and the unlikeness of the Second, does not arise from distance from the First in the relation by which the First stands as effect, since the First is a gathering of two relations: its being cause, and its being effect. What comes to be from the relation of effect does not exist in the same way as what comes to be from the relation of cause, for the cause is always nobler than the effect and prior to it in rank and in nature. Of the First it is said that it is cause, and it is said that it is effect; yet it is a single essence, acquiring these relations through the additions.

**Section Five of the Third Chapter**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

The diminution fell in the soul only because it is farther from the First Cause — by which I mean the Preceding One.

We say:

There is no diminution in the Second — which he calls a soul — as we have already established, nor is it remote from the First; on the contrary, it is his like. The diminution is a necessary attribute, not the very nature of the soul. The soul became deficient not from the side of its own essence, which is its perfection, but from the side of its second perfection, which it acquires by benefit.

**Section Six of the Third Chapter**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Nature's birth from the soul is no greater a step than the soul's birth from the intellect, for the soul, relative to the intellect, is farther removed than nature is relative to the soul. If the soul may be born from the intellect — despite the intellect's perfection, nobility, and nearness to the First Cause — then nature may equally be born from the soul, since nature resembles the soul more closely in all its states, acts, and powers than the soul resembles the intellect in its acts and powers. Among the ancients, nature is defined as the principle of motion; some called it the active power. From either of these definitions, the greater and fuller share belongs to nature. The soul, among the ancients, is the moving, abiding substance, and is characterized by intellect as well. Yet there is nothing in the intellect's definition that belongs to the soul's definition, nor is the soul defined by the definition of the intellect. The intellect is defined as the first of things: the Originated, the first effect, the first intermediary. None of these may be said of the soul — not that it is the first of things, not that it is originated, not that it is the first effect.

If, then, it is permissible that from the intellect — with its perfection, nobility, and nearness to the Word (الْكَلِمَة) — there should be born a likeness of the soul, which is not defined by the intellect's definition (and this cannot be denied), then it is equally permissible that from the soul there should be born a likeness of nature, which resembles the soul in its defining limits (and this too cannot be denied). Had one approached this matter with proper reflection, this insight would not have remained hidden. Had the author of al-Islah attended to the wonders and wisdom contained in nature, and to the splendor, nobility, goodness, and beauty in its acts — qualities by reason of which the partial soul desires to incline toward nature and follow it — he would have known with certainty that nature is born from the soul, though it does not resemble it. For causes always find the order of their effects beautiful, and it is for this reason that the partial soul desires to follow nature. All goodness, splendor, nobility, and adornment come from the higher noble world. Had nature not been born from the soul, it could never have borne witness to goodness, beauty, and adornment. Because it is born from the soul, it declares what it has beheld of beauty and nobility in the world of its cause — a deficient declaration, falling short of the soul's own. Mark this well.

This is his statement.

We say:

The sound clarification of what he has brought is contained in what has already passed in the discourse on the intellect, the soul, and nature, and on the existence of what precedes another in existence, and the rest. There is no need to extend it further by dwelling on the error that has persisted in conception. In that is sufficiency.

We may therefore take up the judgment between the two contenders directly: the question whether the soul is parts or traces, and the discussion that follows from it.

**The First Section**

The author of the Reform said:

According to what the author of al-Nusrah has established: the parts within us are traces of the first essence, not parts of it. Our union is by the traces that come from the first essence, not by its parts. The union of the First is not by its parts, because the First is united by the very Word. The parts within us, though they are traces of the First, are not parts of it, and the First is not united by them; rather, those parts are united by its traces, as we have shown in the union of its products with our traces within them. Nor is the union of the first essence with the Word of this kind, for the first essence is united with the very Word, until it and the Word became one thing. This is his statement.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

This statement holds confusion and manifest contradictions. He said that the parts within us are traces of the first essence — yet how can parts be traces, when they are essences subsisting in themselves? Traces have no subsistence in themselves. If he says that the parts within us are traces of the first essence, then, once the name "parts" has fallen upon them, he is obliged to show that they are parts of some essence. Were they not parts of the first essence, he would not have called them parts of any essence at all. And once it is established that they are parts of some essence, it is void that they should be traces, because the parts of a thing are not traces of another. This is his statement.

We say:

The author of al-Nusrah is right that souls are essences subsisting in themselves after acquisition, and that traces cannot subsist in themselves. Yet the author of the Reform refused to give the souls the name of parthood because he saw that the things which admit of division are the bodies, which are never free of the nine accidents and are grasped by the five senses. The soul is not a body, and that which overflows upon it is not a body either. So he did not see fit to give it the name "part," lest he set it in the course of bodies and misrepresent what the soul's own essence is and what it has disclosed of itself. Since he did not intend that, he said "traces," naming them as things that come to have essence and to endure. What he means is that these souls have their coming-to-essence and their endurance by the traces of those separate essences that reach them from the side of the limits, who are the intermediaries (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). If this is so, then it appears that the intention of the author of the Reform, in saying "traces," is that which runs in the soul in the course of the form: that by which the essentiality of the souls is completed, and by which the soul endures when it receives it. This is what he made necessary where he says: we said only that honor and merit belong to these worlds because we received the trace of that noble essence in full, and were prepared to receive it. So it is established that by "trace" he intends that which is received, and that what the author of al-Nusrah intends by "part" is that which runs in the soul in the course of the hayula — which is that which receives. This is by way of likeness and approximation to the understandings.

**The Second Section**

As for the author of al-Nusrah's claim that the souls are parts of the Universal Soul, it rests upon no proof. For when something is divided, its whole is the sum of all those parts. If he grants this, he has made it necessary that the souls are parts of the Universal Soul. But concerning the souls in the abode of this world, the matter is settled by the proof already established, earlier and later: the Second — which he named the Soul — has its existence not in the abode of the body, which is the abode of this world. Since it is not in this world, it is void that the Second should be a whole for these souls. And once it is void that it be a whole for them, these souls are not parts of it.

**The Third Section**

His assertion that souls are parts of the Universal Soul does not hold together with his intention that the Universal Soul is the Second. For if the souls are parts of the Second, the matter is not free of one of these cases: either the whole of them, which is the Second, is in the abode of this world; or some of them are in it and some in the higher world; or the Second has nothing of parthood in this world at all.

It is void that the whole which is the Second should be in the entire abode of this world. What is in this world subsists by potentiality and has no passage into act except by that which subsists in act. The first Intellect is prevented from being that by which the souls subsisting in potentiality pass into act, because of what this would require of the precedence of that whose existence is impossible for God, glorified be He — upon which the discourse has already passed in a book other than this.

It is likewise void that some of them be in this world and some in the higher world. The part in the higher world, were it like this one in the world, subsisting by potentiality just as this one is, would stand in the very condition of this one. That is void by the proof already established: that the existence of the Second is an existence subsisting in act, not like the existents of this world's abode, which subsist by potentiality.

After the voidness of both divisions, it is established that the Second has nothing of parthood in this world, and it is void that the souls should be parts of it.

**The Fourth Section**

Beyond the matter of the parts, we note that a whole gives to all that is under it what it gives, in all its states, according to itself. So if these souls were parts of the Second, and we have found them neither knowing nor wise, then the whole whose parts they are would be of this same condition. To hold such a thing of that mighty limit is unbelief — we seek refuge in God — when it is known that the substances of the Messengers (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) are from it, and that it is the proximate cause of the overflow upon the lower world. The souls, then, are not parts of the Second.

When it was established as void that these souls could be parts, we said: the souls are of the nature of those separate things whose existence is a creative existence. Their appearance and their existence are only from between the natural world and the world of emanation. The soul is a natural power that attains what it acquires from the side of the limits through obedience and the two worships. From its own self there is emitted an abiding, abstracted form, which resembles the abstracted things in the abode of the Hereafter from one aspect and differs from them from another.

Hence we say: it is the second emanation. Our epistles on the Return (al-Maad) contain the mention of that, God willing.

**The Fifth Section**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Likewise, our traces united with our products do not receive our traces after we have finished the work, nor do the products prepared to receive from us receive any further, except by the entry of corruption into them and their change from their states. They are not parts of us, nor are they essences subsisting in themselves, but rather vanishing accidents. This is his statement.

We say:

What is meant by this is that bodies reach a limit in what they can receive — a limit beyond which they receive nothing further. This is like iron heated in the fire: once it has reddened, that is its utmost, and it grows no hotter. Or like a black body, which grows no blacker, for it may reach in blackness a limit beyond which it is not further blackened. That meaning is more fitting to be held than what his own phrase requires. And it is not the traces that are the receiver; the receiver is other than they, namely the body, which is the substrate for the succession of the accidents and the traces upon it.

**The Sixth Section**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

But the speaking souls within us do not cease to acquire from the light of the higher, noble world, and to increase thereby in nobility within themselves, without any change occurring in themselves, and without the entry of corruption into them from the Soul when it wishes to benefit them. So it is established that they are parts and essences of the Soul, not traces of it.

We say:

That the soul is unbounded in receiving is, as he said, one of the proofs that the soul is not a body. But the matter of the soul being parts of the Second is not as he held, as the discourse above has already shown through what that claim entails and folds within it. The best that can be ascribed to his statement, for one who intends by "parts" this, is that these souls, which are the receiver, when they intellect their own essences as such, are then one thing with what they have intellected: it is they, and they are it, distinguished from it only by rank. So it is like the part of a thing in which is found what is found in the whole of it, their way in their own essence being one and the same from this aspect.

**The Seventh Section**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Also, to say that the speaking souls existing in this world are not parts of the Universal Soul nullifies prophethood, the imamate, the executorship, revelation, and the sacred laws. For it would then not be permitted for the soul to perceive that which influences it, nor to encompass it, nor to benefit from it. Yet the prophets (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) claimed that they beheld the noble upper world, and stood upon the spiritual limits, and benefited from what they conveyed to those after them of light and exposition — from those above them, from the two roots and the three branches — and that they beheld the angels. Were their pure souls only traces of the Universal Soul, they would not have been able to comprehend what was revealed to them, nor to stand upon those spiritual realities that are parts of the Universal Soul.

We say:

The discourse has already established that the souls are neither parts nor traces, and that they are a second emanation. What the one who called them "traces" means is that by which the essentiality of the souls is completed and which earns them endurance. What the one who called them "parts" means is that the souls, by intellecting their own essence as such, are like those things that are their cause. Prophethood is not nullified by this, nor the imamate, nor anything else — for it is established that these ranks are not from this aspect. The prophets (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) were able to perceive those things absent from them of the upper world only after they attained the rank of perfection and became thereby complete at its utmost. When they return to their own essences, it is as though they have perceived those transcendent essences by their very being — they and those essences being, from the aspect of completeness, one thing, with no difference save in rank. We have set out in our book known as Rahat al-Aql enough of that to suffice and to heal, that it may be known.

**The Eighth Section**

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Rather, it is necessary to say that the Intellect is creative through the Word, the Soul is the image of the Intellect, nature is generated from the Soul, and the speaking souls are parts of the Universal Soul — so that by this order tawhid, reward, punishment, prophethood, the imamate, the sacred laws, and revelation are made sound.

We say:

The soundness of tawhid, of reward and punishment, of prophethood and the imamate, of the mission and the laws drawn from revelation — together with their establishment — is not from the aspect that the Intellect is creative through the Word and that the Soul is the image of the Intellect. Their establishment is from another aspect, which we have set out in our epistles and our writings concerning them. As for the Intellect, it may not be said that it is creative through the Word, for that would require the precedence of the Word over the Intellect, with the disorder this brings into the paths of tawhid, according to what we have expounded in our discourse.

Then we say:

The Intellect is nothing but the very Word, and the Word is nothing but the very Intellect. This is confirmed by the statement of our master the Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah (ع) in the book Tawil al-Sharia, where he speaks of the intelligibles: that the Word is an expression of the Intellect, and that it merits these names by relation. There has already passed, in our exposition and our discourse upon the Creator, the Intellect, the Word, and what is said of the world of creation and the first emanation — in the Illuminating Epistle and the other epistles — what suffices the seeker. As for the Soul and nature, they are two emanations from the first Intellect, each according to its own relation. For that reason one became more excellent than the other: the more excellent is the first emanation, the Soul, and the speaking souls are the second emanation. So what occurred in the first of them is emanated in the last of them. Our epistles alone on the Return (al-Maad) contain enough mention of that to make lengthening unnecessary, for the expansion of speech upon the like of this in every place is forbidden, and a gesture suffices the seeking student, while another discards it for the difficulty of its reach and the hardship of knowing it. God grants success to the believing knower for the knowledge of that according to his strength in sincerity to God and to His friends, and aids him when he is sincere to His face, exalted be He, and gives his allegiance to Him and to His friends. May God make us among the followers, the receivers, who fulfill His covenant; and may He grant us success in His praise, by His grace and His glory.

The fifth book of the Riyad concerns the dispute between two thinkers over whether human beings are the fruit of the physical world. That is the question I now take up.

In the first section of this book, the author of al-Islah said:

Man is the fruit of this entire world, and it is for his sake that the world was created in all its parts — its origins and its foundations. The first of these is the Hayula, which is the principle of the individuals born from it by motion and rest; then the individuals, which are the foundation of the vehicles; then the compounds, which are the very productions of this whole world; and the natures from which the human form is composed — a form prepared to receive the three souls: the vegetative, the sensitive, and the speaking.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

To say that human beings are the fruit of this world is the position of the materialists — those who did not affirm the soul's survival after the dissolution of bodies. For if human beings were the fruit of this world, this world would have held them fast and not allowed them to pass into another.

But we would say:

Human beings are the fruit of the highest world, the honorable and luminous world. That is why the prophets (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) came with their warning: so that people might prepare themselves for the passage from the house of mortality to the house of survival, and from this world to the abode of the Return. The prophets knew that this world is no true home and that man is not its fruit. So said the author of al-Nusrah.

We say:

Each of the two is truthful in what he said from one side, and untruthful from another. The side on which they are both truthful is that each has said of human beings what truly belongs to him. The side on which they are both untruthful is that each denies the other its share — denies, that is, that man bears the title of fruit of both worlds together. For human beings issue from between the two worlds. From this world man receives his first perfection, and from that world his second.

The natural world fulfills its purpose by bestowing on its creature the first perfection: the bringing forth of the bodily form by way of the circling bodies, the luminous planets, and the proximate causes, until the creature arrives at the disposition by which it is ready to receive what belongs to it. And how could it not receive this, when it is that world's very fruit — the summit beyond which that world has well nigh nothing? The higher world fulfills its purpose by bestowing on what has been received from the existents of the natural world the second perfection: an effusion upon the spiritual image, that which is naturally disposed and intrinsic to it, by which it becomes substantial and endures. This second perfection is the knowledge of the Oneness of Allah Almighty by means of all the hudud (حُدُود) (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), and obedience to them in the two modes of worship — in knowledge and in deed. That is man's fruit.

What confirms what we have said in this matter is the saying of Mawlana Amir al-Muminin al-Muizz li-Din Allah Maad ibn Ismail (ع) in the book *The Interpretation of Sharia* (كِتَابُ تَأْوِيلِ الشَّرِيعَةِ): that man is the purpose of the second world and the end of the action of nature.

Now to the second section, concerning the objection of the author of al-Nusrah — that if human beings were the fruit of this world, this world would have held them fast and not allowed them to pass from it to another world. By this very objection he has handed his opponent the means to turn the matter back upon him.

For his opponent says:

If, as you have said, man is the fruit of the higher world, then that world would hold him fast and would not let him return to these persons, so that he should forget — which is impossible, according to your own writing and requirement. This is no argument that proves what he intends to demonstrate in the abstract. Neither is the sending of the prophets, whom he urges toward provision, a proof that human beings are the fruit of this world. For the human being who is in truth a human being is such by the conjoining of the effusion of the two worlds: from the natural world, that which runs in the channel of the Hayula, and from the world of the Intellect, that which runs in the channel of the form. The one comes by intermediaries, and the other by intermediaries.

In the third section, the author of al-Islah said:

The Soul emanates from the First Intellect in perfection; the Hayula emanates from the Soul in perfection; and the form emanates from the Hayula in perfection. The whole, therefore, was perfect.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

If the matter is as he has said — that the perfection of the Soul is like that of the Intellect — then his statement about what is spread out upon the Hayula, the form, and the compounds is void and self-contradicting. For it is not permissible to imagine that these fashioned things come to be except from the pairing of two: one perfect and self-sufficient, the other deficient and in need, so that a marriage may take place between them, as is found among things witnessed — such as the heaven and the earth. The heaven is as the male: perfect and self-sufficient in all its motions, its orbits being manifest. The earth is deficient, in the rank of the female, her need for him established. For this reason a marriage took place between them, and from between them appeared the various kinds of metals differing in their forms, and the plants, and the animals — not one of which appears actually in the heaven or in the earth or in the mothers, but which were in them in potency. When they were married, all of them appeared in actuality. Had their state not been as described — one deficient and the other perfect — nothing would have appeared from them. So said the author of al-Nusrah.

We say:

As for the statement of the author of al-Islah — that the Soul is the second, emanating from the First Intellect in perfection — it is correct, as has already been established above. As for his saying that the Hayula emanates from the Soul: we have already shown that its existence is not from the Soul, which is the second, but from the First Intellect. Its existence and the second are together; neither precedes the other, and neither has existence apart from the other except in the soul by way of imagination. Outside the soul they exist only together.

As for the statement of the author of al-Nusrah — that it is not permissible to imagine that the fashioned things come to be except from the pairing of one perfect and self-sufficient with another deficient and in need, so that they may be coupled by what lies between them, and his likening of this to the heaven and the earth — he has refuted himself by the very words that follow. For he says that from between them appeared the various kinds of metals differing in their forms, and the plants, and the animals, not one of which appears actually in the heaven or in the earth or in the mothers, because they were in potency. And this is to say that if any of these things — I mean the generated beings — does not appear actually in the heaven and the earth because it is in potency, then the heaven and the earth are equal in respect of their being in potency, and no superiority of one over the other appears.

It is not the case that when existents come to be from between two things, one of the two must be perfect and the other deficient. We have already shown that deficiency is disclosed in things not in their selves but in their ranks, when some are set beside others, and in their actions, when they do not come to be except by something other than that which completes their existence — while in their selves they are perfect. For if their selves were not perfect in the existence that befits them, no action could proceed from them, neither by themselves nor by another. The condition in which the existents are actually found bears witness to this. The heaven, which he singled out for perfection and artistry, is deficient in its action, since its action is not completed except by that upon which it turns; and the earth, which he singled out for deficiency and need, has its deficiency not in its self but in its action, for its action is not completed except by that which turns upon it. So too with the animal and the newborn. And if this is so, then the saying of the author of al-Nusrah — that the statement of the author of al-Islah is a contradictory and prejudiced statement — is itself the contradictory and prejudiced statement.

In the fourth section, the author of al-Nusrah said:

He did not answer what was raised at the end of this section: that the name of perfection falls upon the Originator, glorified be He, because it falls upon perfect origination.

We say:

The author of al-Islah mentioned nothing of the sort. What he reported from the sages in the book of al-Islah — that they said the perfect Originator has perfect origination, and that the origination which is the perfection could be nothing but perfect — is a saying than which none could be more correct. By that saying he established that the perfect and the perfection are the origination and the originated, not the Originator, glorified be He. The name of perfection, by what he mentioned, does not fall upon the Originator, glorified be He, nor does his speech contain anything of that. The claim of the author of al-Nusrah here is prejudice against the author of al-Islah.

In the fifth section, the author of al-Nusrah said:

We all say that origination is the cause of the originated, and that it and the originated, from the side of the originated, are one thing, and it is perfect; and that what is originated by perfect origination could be nothing but perfect. Nor are we obliged to say that the Originator, glorified be He, is perfect, or that He is a cause, or that He, glorified and exalted, and the originated are one thing.

We say:

That is a statement correct in its meaning, save that we do not say that the originated by perfect origination could be nothing but perfect because origination is the perfection. Rather we say that the originated by the origination which is the perfection could be nothing but perfect; that the originated is the origination; and that it is the cause, the effect, the perfection, and the perfect. These names follow one upon another over it according to the relations, because there is a multiplicity there in the essences, so that the meanings of these names fall upon them all, while the thing there is one. In what we have set down upon this, in this book and in others, there is sufficiency without prolonging.

In the sixth section, the author of al-Nusrah said:

If it is established that this world is the act of the Soul, and that it is withal in the utmost order and arrangement, with perpetual circling motions, then we know and are certain that in her act she sought to attain the rank withheld from her before she began to act. Since this is so, and since there was in the world nothing more honorable than the human being, nor anything more disposed to receive the effects of the Soul from her and in which her benefits are more efficacious, we know and are certain that human beings are the fruit of the Soul's attainment of the end appointed for her from the side of her cause. So understand that.

We say:

It has already gone forth from our speech, in the matter of the perfection of the second — which in his account is the Universal Soul — what indicates that in her act she did not seek to attain a rank she had not gained. The Universal Soul, which is the second, effuses upon this world not to draw to herself what is not hers, for Allah enriched her, when He brought her into being, by perfection, so that she seeks nothing that was not given her. Rather her act is to establish wisdom in the bringing forth of what is in potency into act, and to make what is base excellent, and what is later in existence to follow upon what went before. And whoever considers it well finds that the benefit returns upon that which is brought forth into act, and upon him who is under the charge of striving toward perfection, not upon her who is neither charged nor in need. To believe otherwise of that mighty hadd (حَدّ) is error and sin. And since this is so, and since the human being has two sides — one of them natural and one of them divine — he is neither the fruit of this world purely nor the fruit of that world purely, but the fruit of both worlds together. He is the last in the beings, united with eternity by what he has acquired in time. Therefore it has been said:

> مَا جَرَى فِي أَوَّلِهِمْ، جَرَى فِي آخِرِهِمْ

What came to pass in the first of them came to pass in the last of them.

And whoever has known from that the stations of the prophets, the guardians, the imams, and the righteous (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) is disposed for deliverance. May Allah gather us with our pure masters in the House of Holiness.

As for the seventh section, and the saying of the author of al-Nusrah that every doer does what he does only in seeking to attain what he wills, and especially when the act proceeds from the doer with motion, order, and arrangement, and his holding that this is not binding upon the First Originator and upon origination, because the act there is by way of metaphor, not with motion, nor order, nor arrangement, but rather its first is its last, and its first and its middle are the utmost of its utmost, and its utmost is its middle, there being in it no order and no arrangement; but the order and the arrangement are in that which the second gains, from the lights of Him in whom there is no arrangement and no order, and He is the First Intellect; and the Soul comes to resemble the Intellect greatly, so that when she looks into it toward Him she apprehends the powers of things that are without order and without arrangement, apprehending things rather all at once, and this belongs to her only when she is united with the Intellect and has driven back the material things of dark nature:

We say:

How can what he said be sound, when order and arrangement are found only from the Intellect? And how can it be sound, when the things taken all at once are made excellent only by the Intellect, and the Soul, in which the effects of the Intellect leave no impress, is on a level with the beasts? It is for this reason that Allah has lifted knowledge from the Soul until the time when the effects of the Intellect leave their impress upon her. We have already said above that the proposition concerning doers is not universal, so that not every doer seeks by his act to attain a want or a purpose. What I reckon he intended by that saying is that the essence of the First Intellect is not composite, so as to have arrangement and order. But as for apprehension, the Intellect apprehends only by a true apprehension.

Chapter Eight of the Book of Riyad: On the Judgment between the Two Contenders, of which he spoke in the chapter of Decree and Destiny.

**Section One of Chapter Eight**

The author of al-Islah said:

As for the saying that the decree is prior and the destiny posterior, this is an error, because destiny is before decree, and the prior is before the posterior. It is not permissible that the decree, which comes after destiny, should be identified with that which is before the posterior. Decree and destiny are two words whose meaning is known from ordinary speech: destiny is estimation, and decree is elaboration, and there is no elaboration except after estimation, so the first is before the second by the farthest reach of priority. The witnesses to this from the Book of God are His words:

> قضي الامر الذي به تستفتيان
"The matter concerning which you two sought counsel has been decreed."

meaning that it has been separated out and brought to an end; and His words:

> فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةُ
"When you have finished the prayer,"

meaning, when you have completed it. The decree is like a garment that the tailor first estimates: before he cuts it he estimates it, and he adds and subtracts, widens and narrows; but once he has cut it he has decreed it and made an end of it, and after that no increase in it is possible. That is the likeness of decree and destiny. The upshot of his saying is this: decree is not predicated of the prior, for it comes after destiny; and destiny is not predicated of the posterior, for it comes before decree. Destiny is estimation and decree is elaboration, and as long as the thing remains within estimation it can be increased, decreased, and widened, but once it has passed into elaboration and been decreed, no increase in it and no decrease from it is possible.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Decree is not elaboration, for the state of the very act of elaboration within the decree is no less than the state of the separated thing itself, since the separated thing is fixed upon its form by a decree that requires this, just as the separated thing is likewise established only by what has been decreed for it. As for destiny, it is estimation, as he has said, except that there is no estimation save by a judgment that requires that estimation. As for the witnesses he cited from the Book of God to the effect that decree is a bringing to completion, these are not to be dismissed, for the sages have said: when God, exalted be He, originated the Intellect, He brought the two worlds to completion, since the Intellect is the sum of the images of the two worlds, and nothing of the images of the worlds is absent from the Intellect, so it is pure completion. Yet the author of al-Islah has erred in likening destiny and decree to the garment that the tailor estimates. He made the estimation correspond to destiny and the cutting correspond to the decree, and this analogy does not stand upright. What he ought to have done is to make the image of the sewing that resides in the very soul of the tailor correspond to the decree, because it is spiritual; and the estimation by which the tailor estimates that sewing correspond to destiny, for that too is a spiritual thing that has not yet emerged to the limit of intellect, and this is the meaning of the image of the two origins. Then the cutting which he performs after estimation, upon the bodily boundaries that have emerged from the first and the second, corresponds to what appears in body. If the matter is as we have described, then decree precedes destiny, just as the sewing precedes the estimation, and by that sewing the tailor is made ready for the estimation by which he estimates. So it is established that decree is prior and destiny is posterior. This is the upshot of his saying:

Decree is ahead of destiny, and there is no estimation except by a judgment, so decree is prior and destiny posterior.

We say:

The interpretation the two contenders give of decree and destiny, each according to what he has invoked, is an impossible interpretation, even granting the meaning of the two words as we have shown it, in whatever way they assign decree and destiny to the prior and the posterior. For the author of al-Islah has committed himself, by his saying that destiny is estimation and decree is elaboration, and by the analogy he brought forward in the matter of the garment and the image of the sewing, to holding that destiny is what stands in potency, what could yet be, and that decree is what stands in act, what has already come out from the door of possibility, which is potency, into actuality. Now if this were the meaning of destiny and decree, then it is impossible to predicate them of the prior and the posterior at all, in any respect, since neither of the two stands in potency, nor was in potency and then emerged into act, according to the proofs we have already set down.

**Section Two of Chapter Eight**

The author of al-Nusrah has committed himself, by his saying that there is no estimation except by a judgment that requires that estimation, and by his representing the decree with the craft of sewing from which the estimation proceeds, to making destiny posterior, while yet conceding that the meaning of destiny is, as the author of al-Islah established it, the existence of an existent by potency. But it is not permissible to predicate this of the posterior, since it has been established from what we said above that the posterior already stands in act; and if it were permissible, then destiny would not be posterior. And if destiny is not the posterior, then decree has all the more claim to be the prior, and is even further from being predicated of it, since the posterior was never in potency such that it then went out into act to answer to what its own word conveys of the state of the prior. It is likewise impossible that decree and destiny be predicated of the prior and the posterior. And since this is impossible, we say that the statement of the two men is correct only in the manner we shall now explain, not in the manner to which they went, for decree shares its meaning with several things, and those things all belong to the world of body, not to the world of origination; and likewise destiny.

**Section Three of Chapter Eight**

As for decree, it points, first, to the Speaker who was in potency and then emerged into act by the support of God, exalted be He, and to those who take his place (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), who have reached in their attainment the rank parallel to the first upsurge. All of these, in their standing in act, in their command, prohibition, and decree within the summons that is already established in act, having been in potency, answer to the meaning conveyed by the word "decree" (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). This is what the author of al-Nusrah intends, and upon this his saying and his placing of decree first are sound.

**Section Four of Chapter Eight**

Decree points, second, to what is drawn out by interpretation from the potency of the revelation and the Law, from the sciences that are not set forth explicitly within them but reside within them in potency, into exposition and act, by which souls are brought out from the limit of potency to the limit of act. This is what the author of al-Islah intends by his interpretation of the word "decree."

**Section Five of Chapter Eight**

Decree points, third, to what emerges into act and to the latent unfolding of events and transformations appointed to arise in the world through the movement of the moving things and the stillness of the still, those that admit of no reversal. For this reason it is said, when some matter comes to pass and is realized in act, that there is no repelling the decree of God. These are the things of which decree is predicated.

**Section Six of Chapter Eight**

As for destiny, it points, first, to the promised Qaim (الْقَائِم), foretold and heralded from the time of Adam (ع), and to his summons, whose safekeeping and upholding are borne by the Imams and the Messengers (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) through their summoners in the period of concealment, holding out its force in that he is appointed to come forth from estimation into act and existence. His summons, though established, stands from the side of the ranks of the cycle of the Prophet (ع) and his family in the concealment that runs in the manner of what is standing in potency, not in the manner of the manifest that runs as what is standing in act. For this reason the inner meaning of the Night of Determination, Laylat al-Qadr (ع), is he, and to him point the allusions of the shaykhs in their saying:

كوني قدر
"Be, O destiny."

**Section Seven of Chapter Eight**

Destiny points, second, to what the Prophet (ع) and his family brought from the revelation, the Law, the rulings, and the parables that hold within their potency the sciences and the knowledge the soul needs in its passage to maturity and act, being cast in a form that gathers all of that together. For this reason no complete science is found upon its outer face except through interpretation drawn out of it, and the saying of the author of al-Islah in this direction points to this meaning of destiny.

**Section Eight of Chapter Eight**

Destiny points, third, to the world with all its parts, which has within its power to come forth into being and act through the passage of days, months, years, events, and the coming-to-be whose existence proceeds from it by the perpetual movement of the movers over what is beneath them, of necessity, since these are appointed within it. For this reason it is said: what God has appointed will be, for its coming-to-be is by way of the necessity of its existence; and though the term be long, it is as one already existing in act. So God, exalted be He, said:

> إِنَّهُمْ يَرَوْنَهُۥ بَعِيدًۭا وَنَرَاهُ قَرِيبًا
"They see it as far off, but We see it as near."

Whatever was in estimation, appointed to exist, is decree once it exists, since the word "decree" signals what was in potency and then came out into act. These are the meanings of decree and destiny.

If one ponders the words of the author of al-Islah, and his saying that destiny precedes decree, the soundness of its meaning holds only with respect to what the Prophet (ع) and his family brought of the revelation and the Law, which precedes the decree that is the interpretation, as he himself did and interpreted. And the saying of the author of al-Nusrah, that decree precedes destiny, if it is pondered, its meaning is sound only with respect to the Speaker (ع) who stands in act, who is the decree that precedes what he brought of the revelation and the Law, which is destiny.

**Section Nine of Chapter Eight**

The author of al-Nusrah said, reporting from the learned sages:

When God, exalted be He, originated the Intellect, He brought the two worlds to completion, because it is the gathering place of the images of the worlds.

We say:

The Intellect that is the gathering place of the images of the worlds is not the First originated Intellect, nor the second Intellect, which is the second upsurge; rather it is the Intellect that ascends from the world of nature by acquisition, in deed and in knowledge, to the parallel of the first upsurge, so that it surges a second surging and thereby becomes a compendium of the images of the worlds in all their multitude, its very essence imprinted with the forms of all existents, as is the case with the Enunciators, the Executors, and the Imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). The First Intellect is too exalted to be multiplied by this kind of multiplication, since its existence is originative, and originative existence is multiplied only according to what it intellects of its own essence, namely that it is a cause and an effect, and that its existence is only from that which is beyond itself, from which it received. The remaining existents, I mean the Intellects that surge in a first surging, are multiplied according to what I have said of their essences and of that whose existence precedes them, back to the First Intellect, their existence being, together with this, from that toward which they turned in devotion, which is beyond them. So the later in existence is not multiplied as the prior in existence is multiplied. Its need to be multiplied for the sake of intellecting all existents is a binding necessity, whereas the First in existence is entirely free of that need in the completeness of its being. If this is so, then it is clear that the one which is a compendium of the images of the two worlds is not the First Intellect, but the Intellects that surge from the abode of nature in a second surging.

Then we say:

The First Intellect does not require that it intellect what is beneath it, nor that it form any image, by reason of what its essence is from eternity: completeness, subsistence, unity, and immunity from change. Rather it is so only by reason of that from which it came to be. And since its being is eternal, complete, subsistent, one and singular, immune from transformation, only by reason of that from which it came to be, exalted be He, it is impossible that it intellect anything beneath it, for it has no need of that.

And we likewise say:

The one that is later in existence, from the second surging, is required to intellect what precedes it in existence and so to become a compendium of the images, because the completeness in which its subsistence lies it acquires by its intellecting of that, I mean of what precedes it in existence. And since it needs, for its completeness, its intellecting of that whose existence preceded it among the ranks upon whom the interpretive summons was established, which is the second worship, so that their stations might be made plain, it is required to teach them and to intellect them. And when it teaches them and intellects them, its essence is thereby multiplied from the side of the multitude of its intellected objects, and is unified from the other side, which is its own essence, so that in that unity it resembles what precedes it in existence. Our book known as Rahat al-Aqlِ, The Peace of the Intellect, contains of the evidences of legal proof for this, and of the religious depictions, what suffices and heals the seeker for the sake of his return. May God make us among those who follow His good pleasure in whatever brings distress or delight, and who follow His friends (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) therein.

**Section Ten of Chapter Eight**

The author of al-Islah said:

It is only the error of those who made decree the prior and destiny the posterior. For they found that the learned had named the posterior by the name of destiny, which is indeed its true name, because all the essences surged from the prior in an appointed measure, and that surging was destiny itself, so the sages named it destiny. Then in the speech of the people "decree and destiny" came to be uttered together, and they were found to place decree ahead of destiny in speech, so that one says "this is decree and destiny." The meaning of decree and destiny was hidden from them, so they assigned decree to the first and destiny to the second, and from this side the error occurred. This is as we said: that all the essences surged from the prior in an appointed measure, and that surging was destiny itself, and it is the compendium of the essences. Confirming this is the saying of God, exalted be He:

> إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَهُ بِقَدَرٍۢ
"Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure."

For just as all the essences surged from the First, which is the command in appointed potency, and were destiny itself, so likewise there appeared from the second, in act, out of matter and form, and that act was decree itself. And within destiny there occurs change and alteration, and it is the book of which God, exalted be He, said:

> يَمْحُوا۟ ٱللَّهُ مَا يَشَآءُ وَيُثْبِتُ
"Allah erases what He wills and confirms."

Destiny is the essence of the posterior, as we have said, and decree is its act, because the posterior is what is appointed in measure from the prior. The upshot of his saying in this section is: destiny is the name of the posterior, because all the essences surged from the prior in an appointed measure, as God, exalted be He, said, "Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure," and decree is its act.

The author of al-Islah said:

As for what he invoked concerning decree and destiny from the saying of God, exalted be He, "Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure," he has erred in the interpretation of this verse. Its interpretation is as we shall expound and state, for by it He intends only the pure Ipseity.

We say:

The meaning of إِنَّا, "We," by which He intends the Ipseity, is that which no attribute and no negation of attribute taints; and "everything," كُلَّ شَىْءٍ, by which He intends the Intellect, which is all things; and "We have created it," خَلَقْنَهُ, by which He intends the image of the two worlds among them; and "according to a measure," بِقَدَرٍ, by which He intends the posterior, upon which the settling of the matter rests, so that all the spiritual and bodily images appeared from between the two in the manifest, which is the pen, the tablet, the writing, and the Writer. The Writer stands over against إِنَّا, "We," and He is the pure Ipseity; the Pen stands over against the Intellect, which is the pen of pens; "We have created it" stands over against the Tablet; the writing stands over against the letters that appear upon the Tablet; and "according to a measure" stands over against the Tablet that is receptive to all the forms of the letters. For just as all bodily and spiritual things, the simple and the dense, fall under these intelligible letters that appear from the Writer, by the Pen, upon the Tablet, so likewise all the higher and lower images God, exalted be He, brought forth by means of the Intellect and the Soul, and nothing of them was withheld from between the two, just as nothing of things is withheld from the ordered letters that appear in act from the Writer upon the Tablet. This is the saying of the author of al-Nusrah in refutation.

We say:

The two contenders have brought forward in this section what cannot stand firm, neither for this one in his emendation, nor for that one in his refutation. For the author of al-Islah, when he held that destiny is the name of the posterior and argued for it by the saying of God, exalted be He, "Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure," has already been met by what preceded in the discussion of destiny and decree, from which it is grasped that destiny may not be predicated of the posterior. And the author of al-Nusrah made his counter to the author of al-Islah's saying rest upon what he interpreted from the verse, and this is neither balanced against nor congruent with the matter. For he said, interpreting:

God, exalted be He, by إِنَّا, "We," intends only the pure Ipseity that no attribute and no negation of attribute taints. But the word إِنَّا, "We," is only at the limit from whose side the Prophet draws supply by his standing in the divine place within the world, not the pure Ipseity itself. And how could "We" fall upon the pure Ipseity, when between Him and it lies the intermediary of utter negation? Rather it falls upon the near intermediary of the Messenger of God (ع) in the outpouring upon him, and the meaning is the Messenger, since he is the one who conveys on His behalf.

**Section Eleven of Chapter Eight**

He said:

"Everything," by which he intends the Intellect, which is all things. But "everything" in this place is not the Intellect, for we have already shown that the First Intellect is not multiplied as that whose existence is "everything" is multiplied, which is what the community needs of the two comprehensive worships that gather the sciences, outwardly by deed and inwardly by the conception that leads to deliverance from the torment of the two worlds.

**Section Twelve of Chapter Eight**

He said:

"We have created it," by which he does not intend what he went to, for "We have created it" means "We have appointed it in measure." I mean: We have made the form of the revelation and the Law a form within whose potency lies everything of the sciences and the religious works the community needs to ward off pains from the soul in this world and the next. It is as though He said, speaking on behalf of God, exalted be He: "We, everything We have created according to a measure," of the matter of the two worships in knowledge and deed which the community needs in its religion and its worldly life, We have appointed in measure within what We brought of the revelation and the Law, an appointing; that is, We placed it within its potency, that it might come forth, in interpretation, to the one who merits it.

**Section Thirteen of Chapter Eight**

As for the saying of the author of al-Islah that decree is the posterior act, he has hit the mark from the side that what comes out into act from the world of nature comes out by its outpouring, and by it is completed, and from its side attains completeness. For this reason decree came to be predicated of the Speaker, since his coming out into act and his attaining perfection are by its outpouring and its support.

**Section Fourteen of Chapter Eight**

He said:

All the essences surged from the prior in an appointed measure. In this there is a contradiction, for the posterior is an essence, and it is surged from the prior, yet it is not appointed in measure. What is meant by his saying is rather that surging from which the bodily world came to be, which is appointed in measure so that things might come from it, as we explained in the chapter of destiny, not the posterior.

**Section Fifteen of Chapter Eight**

As for the saying of the author of al-Nusrah, in the passage where at its head stands "We have created it," by which he intends the image of the two worlds from between them, and "according to a measure," by which he intends the posterior upon which the settling of the matter rests, so that all the spiritual and bodily images appeared from between the two: the matter in the existence of things is not such that what is bodily was and what is non-bodily was, in the manner he mentioned, by reason of the corruption we have shown in the foundation upon which he built his speech. And were it not that discourse upon the order in which the existence of existents rests upon the First lies outside the bound of writing, we would have brought it, and its mention will not fail to appear, God willing, in our epistles and our books.

**Section Sixteen of Chapter Eight**

The author of al-Islah said:

As for the interpretation of the saying of the Messenger of God (ع):

> أَفِرُّ مِنْ قَضَاءِ اللَّهِ إِلَى قَدَرِهِ
"I flee from the decree of God to His destiny,"

he meant only to flee from the subtle support of the prior to the exposition of the posterior, as a man flees from fire, which is a sign of support, to water, which is a sign of exposition. For he wished to flee from the thing that has already been sealed and decreed, whose repelling cannot be contrived, to destiny, which has not yet been decreed.

This is the account, and it is not well-ordered. For the Messenger of God (ع) fled from the decree of God to His destiny for a cause, and the cause was the leaning wall whose falling he feared, so he hastened his step and said, "I flee from the decree of God to His destiny," and he wished to strike for them a parable. The leaning wall is a structure that has leaned so as to fall, and it stands for one of the ranks who has resolved upon some breaking of covenant and hypocrisy and has inclined from obedience to transgression; for when he breaks his covenant he falls from his station, as God, exalted be He, said:

> فَوَجَدَا فِيهَا جِدَارًۭا يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ فَأَقَامَهُۥ
"So the two of them found in it a wall about to fall, and he set it up straight,"

meaning one of the ranks who had resolved upon hypocrisy and rupture, and he set him upright until he stood firm and did not fall to ruin and did not collapse. Just so was the leaning wall past which the Messenger of God (ع) hastened his step: he had recognized one of the ranks who had sensed

The author of al-Islah completed his point: to set a man upright signifies the speed of his walking, for to follow a man in his walking means the statement, the proof, the haste, and the quickness of pace. The Messenger of God (ع) would address those bent on hypocrisy with outward preaching and warning, not with the inner declaration. The measure governs the outward, as we have explained, and the decree governs the inward. His fleeing from the decree of God to His measure was on account of this wall — wary lest it fall, wary for himself — and not a fleeing from the dignity God Almighty had bestowed on him, nor from the degree to which God had raised him.

The author of al-Nusrah said:

He is, upon the seeking of increase, the more eager.

The words *Flee from God's decree to His measure* are not to be interpreted as the author of al-Islah imagines — that the Messenger was fleeing from the rank of the Follower to the rank of the Preceder. By his own claim, the prophets (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) forever seek ascent, and the seeking of height is not the seeking of depth. We say, by the help of God Almighty and His blessing, that the meaning here turns on three senses, and each one establishes that the decree belongs to the Preceder and the measure to the Follower.

The first, and it is the greatest, the most fitting, and the most exact in meaning: what is intended by his fleeing from the decree of God to His measure is this. From the Preceder, God willing, comes the support; from the Follower comes the structuring; from the Speaker comes the composing of the Law; and from the Foundation comes the interpretation of the whole. The interpretation, which is the end, most resembles the support, and the composing most resembles the structuring. The Speaker (ع), in this saying, was making plain that his composing of the Laws resembles the Follower in its structuring of the world — and that he does not resemble the Preceder. He fled from the decree of God, which is the Preceder, refusing to liken himself to it in the origination of support, and turned toward his measure, which is the interpretation, to which he likened himself.

The second sense: his informing his community that he draws benefit from the First by means of the Second, so that in everything he wished to stand upon from the First, he returned to it by way of the Second. It is as if he said: In all that I wish to grasp, I return to the one who is the link between me and the Intellect — and that is the Second.

The third sense, and it is the most honored: what the author of the book (ع) mentioned — his fleeing from the intensity of the light of the support of the Preceder toward the support of the Follower, since al-Jadd (اَلْجَدّْ), with his spiritual power, could not bear it without his very identity nearly dissolving. That is his saying in the story of Moses (ع). This is their statement.

We say:

The author of al-Islah, in interpreting the verse, took a course that conforms to how the matter truly stands concerning the decree and the measure, and it is well done. Better still had he said this: the Prophet (ع) was a prophet who reported hidden things — the events of existence, what was yet to come, what lay within men's breasts — by what God Almighty had singled out for him of revelation. He wished to make plain how what al-Jadd cast to him was opened to him. So he said: I return — which is his saying, *I flee.* I mean: through al-Jadd I cross, from the side of the ranks of God Almighty, the whole of what is on the point of coming to be among the happenings and events of existence — this is the decree of God that inevitably goes forth into act — toward His measure, which is God's creating of the souls and the horizons and their motions that point to what He has measured within them to be, so that what has been made plain in the door of revelation is opened to me. For this God Almighty said:

> سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَتِنَا فِى ٱلأٓفَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ

We shall show them Our signs upon the horizons and within their own selves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.

And He said of those who reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth:

> رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَذَا بَطِلًۭا

Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.

This does not merely point to whether a thing exists early or late among the events of being; rather it points to that thing and gives it utterance. It is as if he said: In what al-Jadd casts to me, I turn wholly to the measure, so that it is glimpsed or opened by taking form before me and being pictured to me. That is his saying: *I flee from the decree of God to the measure.* This is a kind of revelation, and the book *Rahat al-Aql* contains the explanation of it.

### The Seventeenth Section of the Eighth Chapter

The manner in which the author of al-Nusrah pursues his answer reveals his surrender to the author of al-Islah. He brought forward nothing to overturn what al-Islah built his argument upon, except the three meanings he adduced, reckoning them his own. He held that each of them establishes that the decree belongs to the Preceder and the measure to the Follower — not because the Speaker resembles the Follower in his composing of the Law, as al-Islah argued, but because the Speaker returns, in all he wishes to grasp, to the Follower. Even were he to establish this, it would still oblige him to establish that the decree belongs to the Preceder and the measure to the Follower, and yet there is no correspondence at all between the decree and the measure on the one hand and the meanings he set out on the other. Had the meaning of the decree and the measure conformed to the state of the First and the Second — fitted to them from some angle — it would have been allowable to say that the decree and the measure fall upon them from that angle. But the decree means what has already been said of it, and so too the measure, and it is not fitting to predicate these of the First and the Second, for they are free of what the meaning of these two terms would require. Whoever applies them in this way is like one who says of honey, whose nature is sweetness, that it is aloes, whose nature is bitterness.

### The Eighteenth Section of the Eighth Chapter

His likening, in the second sense, the Speaker to the Follower does not conform to the law of the guiding call. Within the world of body and the world of religion, the Speaker holds the station of the Preceder, and the station of the guardian in both of them corresponds to the station of the Follower in the world of origination. The Speaker and the Foundation are thus two likenesses of the Preceder and the Follower, and two likenesses of the sun and the moon.

### The Nineteenth Section of the Eighth Chapter
