And if you draw seven lines, six openings appear from among them, according to these likenesses: one, two, three, four, five, six. And were the analogy to be drawn upon that.

Were the analogy to hold — that the first Speaker has no law — then five openings would have to appear among the seven lines. But six openings appeared among those seven lines. By this reckoning, the seven lines became the masters of the seven cycles, the six openings became the six laws, and the law was made obligatory upon Adam (ع).

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Regarding the chapter of the six openings among the seven lines, and the inference drawn from the lines upon the Prophets and from the openings upon the six laws: the matter is not as he stated. The seven lines stand for the higher letters, since every Prophet inscribed one of those letters; and the six openings stand for the cycles of the Imams — between Adam and Noah, the seven Imams of the first cycle; between Noah and Abraham in the second cycle; between Abraham and Moses in the third; and so on up to Muhammad (ع). No further cycle remains for the two Qaims except the cycle of their successors and substitutes in the world. Thus six openings fell across five lines, inasmuch as between the cycles of the Imams there fell five Speakers who were the masters of the laws, in this likeness:

Adam - Noah - Abraham - Moses - Jesus - Muhammad - al-Qaim
the foundation - the foundation - the foundation - the foundation - the imams - the imams - the imams

Just as no Imams come after the Qaim (ع), he is not charged with establishing the law. And likewise, since no Imams came before Adam (ع), Adam too was not charged with establishing the law. For if establishing the law must be preceded by Imams, it must equally be followed by them. The foundation of Noah (ع) preceded the cycle of Adam's foundation, so Noah was followed by Imams, and therefore the duty of establishing the law fell to him. The same holds for Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). But the Qaim (ع) was preceded by the cycle of Muhammad (ع) and is followed by no Imams; therefore the duty of establishing the law does not fall to him. Likewise, Adam was followed by the Imams of his cycle but was preceded by no Imams; therefore the duty of establishing the law did not fall to him. This is what they say.

We say:

The statement of the author of al-Islah agrees with what he has indicated, save for one passage within his words — his saying that "just as the opening appeared after the second line, so the law of the first was not fulfilled except by the appearance of the second Speaker." This is an unsound saying and not upright. The law of Adam (ع) is itself its own foundation, and it was Adam who raised up its foundation. If it were permissible to say that the law of Adam was not fulfilled until the coming of the Speaker who holds the second cycle, it would likewise be permissible to say that the law of Muhammad (ع) is incomplete and is fulfilled only by the coming of the Qaim, who holds the seventh cycle (ع) — and that is among the things impossible to say, for the law is a completed stature that admits no increase and no decrease. Had the author of al-Islah said instead that the first cycle, which belongs to Adam (ع), was not fulfilled except by the appearance of the holder of the second cycle, who is Noah (ع) — and that likewise no cycle is fulfilled except by the appearance of the one that follows it — placing "the first cycle" in the position of his phrase "the law," his words would have been consistent and balanced. And Allah forgives us and him through His mercy.

Chapter Twenty-Eight of Title IX

As for the saying of the author of al-Nusrah concerning the line and the opening, and his interpretation of the six openings upon the Imams: it is sound, provided that the lines stand for the Speakers and not for the higher letters, and that the openings stand for the duration of their command in the cycle and not for the foundations. Even so, this does not require that Adam (ع) have no law. On the contrary, it makes the law obligatory precisely through the presence of the Imams after him. For the Imams are present in order to preserve the station of the Speaker, his law, and his designs within his community; were it not for that purpose, no obedience to an Imam after a Speaker would be obligatory. As for the five lines and the six openings, the author of al-Islah may take them and set the lines upon the five Possessors of Resolve and the openings upon the cycles of the masters of the six laws, since the foremost thing in interpretation is that the thing be identical and balanced when it is stated, so that its place in the souls is the more exalted.

In sum, we say:

The cycle is of two kinds: a major cycle and a minor cycle. The major cycle belongs to the Speakers, whose place the Imams after them preserve within their community. The minor cycle belongs to the completing foundations, who seal the weeks. If the lines are interpreted upon the masters of the major cycles — that is, the Speakers — then the openings can only be the duration of their governance of their community through the Imams who come after them in the cycle, a cycle sealed by the coming of the last of their kind; and its measure is known. If they are interpreted upon the masters of the seven minor cycles — that is, the completing Imams in every cycle — then the openings can only be the duration of the command of the Imams in each week, together with their completers whose cycle is sealed by the seventh of them; and their number is known, as is the number of Imams in each cycle, and the number of the appendages according to the existing higher bodies already described. This will be set down in another book, if Allah the Exalted permits.

Chapter Twenty-Nine of Title IX

The author of al-Nusrah said:

By way of example, the words of Allah the Exalted:

> كَمَا بَدَأَكُمْ تَعُودُونَ
"As He originated you, so shall you return."

That is: as the beginning of the matter was — which was not from the side of the realities — so shall the end of the matter be.

We say:

Even if this is an interpretation, its proper face is to say what corresponds. The words of Allah the Exalted refer to what comes to pass after the Qaim (ع): the return of knowledge, after its going forth into act and its abundance, to potency and to fewness; and the coming of all people after him to be as they were in the time of Adam; and the return of ignorance, after its having been in potency and fewness, to act and to abundance — by reason of the measured wisdom therein. Blessed be Allah, the best of creators.

Chapter Thirty of Title IX

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Again, had the author of al-Islah considered what lies within his name — I mean Adam — by way of indication that he had no law, that would have become plain to him. For his name consists of three letters: Alif, Dal, and Mim (اَلِفٌ، دَالٌ، مِيمٌ). These letters are neither compounded nor composed; each stands apart from the others. This is a clear indication that Adam was not the author of the composition of the law. But the five Prophets who came after him have names that are composed and compounded — such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad (نُوحٌ، إِبْرَاهِيمُ، مُوسَى، عِيسَى، مُحَمَّدٌ) — which is evidence that each of them was the master of a law. This is what he said.

We say:

If the separateness of the letters of Adam's name requires that Adam (ع) have no law, then the fact that these letters are not in themselves separate requires that he have a law. The Alif of the name is composed of alif, lam, and fa (اَلِف، لَام، فَاء); the Mim is composed of mim, ba, and mim (مِيمٌ، بَاءٌ، مِيمٌ); and the Dal likewise. If separateness does not oblige a law for him, then non-separateness does oblige a law. Yet inference of this kind is an impossibility and does not hold. Were it sound, it would follow that the Qaim (ع) is the author of composition, since his name, as the Prophet (ع) reported it, is Muhammad — and Muhammad is composed of four letters. And since it is impossible that the Qaim be the master of a law while his name is composite, it is equally void that the separateness of the letters of Adam's name should indicate that he is not the author of composition and of a law — just as it is void that the joining of the letters of the name of the Qaim (ع), who is Muhammad, and its being composite, should indicate that he is the master of a law. When that is void, no weight attaches to inference of this sort. The law of Adam (ع) is established, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.

Chapter Thirty-One of Title IX

The author of al-Islah said:

As for the saying that Noah (ع) was the first to raise up his foundation, and the likening of him to the ship, enough has already been said of it in the chapter on the foundations.

We say:

Noah (ع) was singled out by the ark because he was the first of the Possessors of Resolve and the first to undertake the abrogation of the laws and to compose a new law. His law stood in the station of the ship, and that by which he abrogated the former law stood in the station of the flood — for by the flood he destroyed the people of the earth, save those who answered his law and boarded his ship, that is, who established obedience to his foundation. The meaning is that his law endured through his lifetime; and when he had perfected it, he committed the matter to his foundation, commanded him to raise up the summons upon his law, and commanded the appendages to hearken to him, so that they attained the flowing grace only through him. Whoever obeyed his foundation was in the ship, and whoever disobeyed him and held to the first law was drowned. Do you not see that those who worshipped Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq, and Nasr (وَدّاً، وَسُوَاعاً، وَيَغُوثَ، وَيَعُوقَ، وَنَسْراً) were described as drowned by the flood? For He said:

> مِنْ خَطِيئَاتِهِمْ اُغْرِقُوا فَاُدْخِلُوا النَّارَ
"Because of their sins they were drowned, then made to enter the Fire."

The author of al-Nusrah said, and we say:

If the station of the ship is like the station of the outward law, then whoever held to it from among the people of the outward was saved — and the veiled, true summons is annulled. Moreover, what is outward in the Book of Allah the Exalted is other than what the author of al-Islah maintained. For Allah the Exalted described the beginning of the command of Noah (ع), his being sent to his people, his calling them to his law, and then commanded him to fashion the Ark. This account is set down in the Sura of Hud; and had the ship been the outward law, Allah would have commanded him first to fashion the Ark. But the story turns upon the fact that Noah first composed the outward law and called creation to make use of it, and only then was commanded to fashion the Ark — meaning, to raise up his legatee. The evidence of this is the words of Allah the Exalted:

> وَٱصْنَعِ ٱلْفُلْكَ
"And fashion the Ark,"

up to His words:

> وَكُلَّمَا مَرَّ عَلَيْهِ مَلَأٌۭ مِّن قَوْمِهِۦ سَخِرُوا۟ مِنْهُ
"And whenever a company of his people passed him, they mocked him" —

meaning that whenever Noah (ع) raised up his legatee, the nobles of his people mocked him and marveled at him, because he was the first to inaugurate the raising up of the legatee; and for that they mocked him. This is what they said.

We say:

As for the saying of the author of al-Islah and his interpretation of the ship upon the outward of the new law: whoever entered beneath its rulings found it to be for him in the station of a ship, delivering him from abasement, humiliation, and every kind of affliction, just as the one within a ship is delivered from drowning; and this meaning is admissible. As for the author of al-Nusrah and his interpretation of the ship upon the summons and the legatee: whoever entered the guiding summons and bound himself to obedience to the foundation was made safe from drowning in error — from turning away from the unity of Allah the Exalted and the knowledge of His limits — that summons being for him in the station of guidance. Both interpretations are sound in this respect, the one in the matter of this world and the other in the matter of religion, and neither of them diminishes the other, for each of them stands upon its own head.

Chapter Thirty-Two of Title IX

As for the saying of the author of al-Nusrah that Noah was the first to raise up the legatee — by the interpretation that came to him — it does not hold. For the prophethood of Adam (ع) and his law are established, and it is confirmed that Seth (ع) was his legatee, the foremost in the law and its establisher under him. Reason itself indicates that each of the Speakers must of necessity have a legatee who takes his benefit from him, especially since every mover of necessity has a moved, the mover being one even if many are moved from him. And since the Speaker in his age is a mover of all souls by his summons to seek subsistence through the raising up of the two worships, he must of necessity have a moved who runs in the course of a learner from him, even if many learners learn from him; and the true learner from him is the one whom we name the legatee. Adam, being a Speaker, must have had a legatee, and so must every Speaker. And since Adam did raise up a legatee for himself, it is not permissible to hold any belief that contradicts that.

Chapter Thirty-Three of Title IX

The author of al-Nusrah said:

Following his interpretation of what Allah the Exalted related concerning the son of Noah:

> سَـَٔاوِىٓ إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍۢ يَعْصِمُنِى مِنَ ٱلْمَآءِ
"I shall take refuge on a mountain that will shield me from the water,"

and Noah's reply:

> لَا عَاصِمَ ٱلْيَوْمَ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ
"There is no shield today from the command of Allah" —

he held that the matter was, before Noah, in the hands of the appendages, since the son did not know the rank of the legatee; and that had Adam possessed a legatee, his son would have known of it. This is what he said.

We say:

This saying of his contradicts what he himself said in the chapter of the cycles: that the Imams after Adam (ع) took charge of his cycle. I do not know how this escaped him. I suspect that the copy of the book has been altered — added to and diminished — through the fewness of those who attend to the matter of religion and their neglect of correcting what they write by collation and by reading it back to the people of knowledge and religion. And Allah is the one whose help is sought.

The interpretation of "the son of Noah" is that this son ascribed to Noah was not of his loins. Rather, he was a man of great worldly standing whom Noah had advanced — like the adversary in the cycle of Muhammad our Prophet (ع). He took his benefit from Noah, learned what Noah had, and by his own strength became a son to him in rank, so that he reckoned it within himself, and the people too imagined that he would be his legatee. But when the command of Allah the Exalted came — that Noah fashion the Ark, that is, that he confer the legateeship upon another below him in accordance with what Allah had commanded — Noah called the people who followed him to enter beneath his command and obedience. That is His saying:

> ٱرْكَبُوا۟ فِيهَا
"Embark in it."

So this man held back from what the others had entered into — obedience to his foundation — refusing to enter the ship. Noah (ع) called him with these words:

> يا بني اركب معنا ولا تكن مع الكافرين
"O my son, embark with us, and be not with the disbelievers" —

calling him to obedience and to binding himself to the command, especially with the desire that he return to his beginning, reckoning that he would act as Noah had seen of his former goodly compliance with his commands. But upon Noah's calling him, and his despairing utterly of that rank he had hoped for, he grew hypocritical and arrogant and refused to obey his foundation in what had come to pass. Noah said that the command of Allah lay upon him: were he not to relinquish his headship, it would be nullified; and the like of this adversary inclined against our guardian (ع). Noah admonished him at one time and warned him at another, saying that the command of Allah lay in it, and that if he did not heed the admonition his headship would depart and abasement would encompass him, and he would see none to take his part nor to help him in his affair; and that is His saying:

> لَا عَاصِمَ ٱلْيَوْمَ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ
"There is no shield today from the command of Allah."

When the son heard this from him, he showed rebellion and said, in his ignorance, that this matter would not be brought to completion for Noah, that he should set the whole of the headship within his own house; and that even if constraint and injury and harm appeared, he would be supported by chiefs who would strengthen his hand and help him to ward off abasement from himself; and that is his saying:

> سَـَٔاوِىٓ إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍۢ يَعْصِمُنِى مِنَ ٱلْمَآءِ
"I shall take refuge on a mountain that will shield me from the water."

The water here is that which is poured out upon the force that slays, and the mountain is that which he clings to of men and partisans. So he set his purpose, and he and his like took up his cause, and they perished in his cycle, and there remained only those who bound themselves to obedience to his foundation.

Allah has set down such tidings in His noble Book as an admonition to the community concerning what befalls the command of the foundation through him who is intransigent toward it and does not bind himself to its obedience. Now He indicates it through our Prophet's word, "O children of Adam"; now He points to it by the she-camel of Salih; and now by the son of Noah — that they may know that the states of the cycle of Muhammad are like the states of the bygone cycles, and that He did not single out Muhammad and his foundation (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) with the intransigence of their community toward them and its hostility toward them. This is a custom that has run through all the Prophets and legatees, reaching to the time of the seventh. The refuge sought by the son of Noah was not to the appendage, but to the people of the outward who were in a state of hypocrisy like his own; he sought their aid, and the sword encompassed them by the power of Allah, and Allah purified the earth of them. That is the flood that overspread outwardly and inwardly. So likewise shall it be in the cycle of Muhammad (ع): some of it has already come true and passed, and some of it shall come true and come to pass by the leave of Allah, and none knows that save the discerning one among the people of the Alawi summons, whose lights Allah has spread abroad.

chapters.before_md:
The Creator of the Thing and the No-Thing

The First Section of the Tenth Chapter

We say:

The author of al-Mahsul, may Allah have mercy on him, when he exerted himself, and strove, and discharged the right of the dawa and its sons, and opened the doors of the landmarks by what he composed of his books that stand over their expanses; and when Sheikh Abu Hatim, may Allah have mercy on him, corrected of it what he corrected: most people supposed that this correction was a fault in the author of al-Mahsul, and so they attacked him on account of the apology which the author of the correction made for that in his book. They faulted it and overturned it. That is a corrupt judgment, an act inclining away from the truth, and the matter is other than what they imagined.

For the speaker (ع), when he knew, at the time of laying down the order of things, that the sciences of religion are too many for a single soul beneath the imam to encompass, or to be able to preserve them all in a single utterance, arranged for them many persons beneath the imamate, that they might cooperate among themselves over all the sciences, their awareness, and their retention, like the twelve hujjas. So each of them benefits, from those to whom Allah the Exalted has entrusted the reins of guidance among the righteous imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), in the abstruse matters, their inner and their outer, according to their capacities and their strength in reception and deduction, that they might be to others in guidance as the imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) are in exposition and instruction. Religion, through them, is like a single person who gathers his parts together, and they are to it like the senses that perceive things: if one of them misses something, another perceives it, without this second perception being a defect against the one that missed the perception, or against the others.

If that is so, then Abu Hatim's correction, may Allah raise his degree, of what he corrected from the book of al-Mahsul, is no fault against him, nor a deficiency against the author of al-Mahsul, nor a challenge against either of them. It is only what we have said: that the persons ranked for the correction of the sciences of religion are like the senses. If one of the senses misses to perceive some thing of the world of nature, the other does not miss it, but cooperates over it, discharging the right of religion and confirming the obligation owed to the Lord of the Worlds.

Since that is so, and since I have seen in the book of al-Mahsul what was most binding upon Abu Hatim, most obligatory for him to expound and to correct, which he did not correct, nor speak upon, but passed over, the truth of cooperation obliged me to discharge the right of religion by clarifying what is folded within what he brought forward, of what it is not permissible to hold as belief in the chapter of monotheism and the first Creator (الْمُبْدِع الْأَوَّل), apart from the other branches which, if Allah aids by deferring the term, we shall discuss in other than this book. So I did it. It is not permissible for me to apologize for that, since the souls are, for religion, all one, even if I apologize to my own soul. Allah accepts from us what we offer to draw near to Him of the guardianship (walaya) that leads to the good pleasure of Allah, Lord of the Worlds, and gathers us, by His grace, both the past and the renewed, the foremost of us and the latecomer, with our pure loyalists (mawali) in the Abode of Holiness; He is Munificent, Generous.

The Second Section of the Tenth Chapter

The author of al-Mahsul said:

In the chapter of monotheism: He is the Creator of the thing and of the no-thing, the rational, the illusory, the intellectual, the logical. I mean what falls beneath these elements, and what does not fall beneath them.

We say:

By this saying he has necessitated that among the existents which are from Allah the Exalted, falling beneath His origination (إِبْدَاع), there is that which is not perceived by reason, nor by illusion, nor by thought, and of which no report is given by logic. Yet its existence is impossible, while he would make belief in it licit. For that which is not perceived by reason, illusion, or thought, and of which logic gives no report, if it had existence, could not but be either prior to the intellect in its existence, or with the intellect in its existence, or posterior to the intellect in its existence.

It is impossible that it be prior to the intellect, for the intellect is the very act behind which is none but Allah the Exalted, from whom it issued and from whom it came to be. It is pure origination, and the true existence (اَلْوُجُودُ الْحَقُّ) which is the first existent from Allah, glory be to Him.

It is impossible, too, that its existence be together with the very intellect; for the intellect is the very intellect that is the origination, and the intellect, at its coming-to-be, is but a single essence, not two. Further, were its existence to be with the intellect, they being distinct yet sharing in existence, it would follow that Allah the Exalted, from whom it came to be, is a manifold originating cause, or that there is with Him another; exalted is He above that with a great exaltation. For it belongs to the effect that its existence be according to its cause, and their being two distinct effects requires two causes, or a cause made manifold by relations, such that the existence of each of them is from a relation within it other than the other's, primarily. So it is impossible that two distinct effects exist from a single cause whose essence is preserved from difference by relations and additions. And if its existence with the intellect requires this, then its existence is impossible, for Allah the Exalted is sanctified above every mode of multiplicity, and additions, and othernesses, and above whatever would make Him a cause.

It is impossible, too, that its existence be posterior to the intellect; for were its existence posterior to the intellect and from it, then knowledge of it would not escape the minds, nor would its definition be hard for them. Rather they would perceive it and define it, just as they defined all the other existents, sensible and intelligible, in the arena of affirmation and negation. Since, then, in its existence it is not free of the three divisions, and each division of them necessitates that its existence be impossible, it is established that its existence is impossible, and to hold it is misguidance.

The Third Section of the Tenth Chapter

Then, had the author of al-Mahsul not said, following his affirmation of the thing and the no-thing, that Allah originated them both, I mean what falls beneath these elements and what does not fall beneath them, we would have said that by "the thing" he intended what is described among bodies, and by "the no-thing" what is not described with the attributes of bodies, from the world of origination, upon the error of him who says that, believing it. But since he brought forward what folds within it the affirmation of the impossible, it resulted only in one's believing, among the existents, in something that shares with Allah in His transcendence in some manner, so that corruption becomes general. And we have shown that this is impossible.

Then we say:

"The thing" is known to be a common term under which fall all the existents, of substances and accidents, sensible and intelligible. His intention in his saying "the no-thing" cannot but be either what some of the sages held, that it is an affirmation of that which is other than a thing, an affirmation stripped of what confines the thing to all its two divisions, of substances and accidents, and raised to the corrected form of the privative proposition, and they alluded to it, saying: that is like our saying "not-the-man," which is an affirmation of everything that is not a man, whereby the one reported of is stripped from us by existence, without affirming what belongs to no thing. They said: it belongs to the particle لا, when by it is intended a specific entity so as to remove it from existence, negating it of that which it is, without affirming of it something other than itself, as in his saying "the thing," which is a universal entity under which every existent falls: when we intend it by the particle لا, we say لا شيء, and the very entity of the thing becomes made to vanish from that in which it is a thing, without affirmation, it being other than it. Or, if by it is intended a particular entity within that entity, and something other is affirmed:

then if his intention is the affirmation of that which is a not-thing, his saying that Allah is its originator is an error. For the no-thing, being that which no attribute befalls, and which is not in a state like that of being a substance or an accident, and the negation of the attributes of the thing from Allah the Exalted being a transcendence and a sanctification, He, the Exalted, being neither substance nor accident, then the attributes of the thing are no attribute of His, nor from Him, nor is He, the Exalted, like them. So it is as though by his saying "the originator of the thing and the no-thing" he said: the originator of His own essence, which is other than the thing, and the originator of the thing, which is other than His essence. And that is an error.

And if his intention is the negation of the very entity of the thing, his saying that Allah the Exalted is its originator is an error. For the thing is the origination, and it is the very entity of existence, and the no-thing is the negation of origination and the nullification of existence. And if the no-thing is the negation of origination, how can it be sound that He is its originator, when He has negated it from that impossible thing?

The Fourth Section of the Tenth Chapter

The author of al-Mahsul said:

The Originator of things, not from a thing; He alone, and no thing with Him, everlastingly. So when we say "He, and no thing with Him," we have negated the thing and the no-thing, and made them both originated; and we have negated every form, simple and composite, from His identity (huwiyya); and we have made everything upon which speech falls, or upon which speech does not fall, an originated effect in truth, finite; and that the no-thing is after the thing, since the coming-to-be of its name came to be only at the appearing of the thing.

We say:

Enough has already passed of the discourse upon the no-thing. His saying, "the Originator of things, not from a thing only, He and no thing with Him, everlastingly," folds within it what is not permissible to hold as belief. For "no-thing" is, with the sages, the affirmation of that which is not a thing, according to what we have mentioned. So when he says "He, and no thing with Him," it is as though he said "He, and that which is not a thing, with Him, everlastingly," and that is associationism (الشِّرْك).

In sum: there is not, among the tongues existing between mankind, that by which expression can be made of Allah the Exalted in a manner befitting Him. For all that the composed and simple words and letters announce is originated, and words, letters, and languages are instruments for mankind in making one another understand what is within themselves. They are originated, and they indicate only what is, like their own state, originated, as we have explained in our treatise known as al-Rawda.

He, the Exalted, being beyond the minds and the perceptions, and behind a veil from the understandings and thought, the ways of inquiry are cut off short of Him. When one is driven to affirm Him, after the knowledge that all that the tongues pronounce and the lips move with falls upon what He has originated and brought into being, glory be to Him, there is no expression borrowed for affirming Him without affirming an attribute or a plurality, save the expression هو, which Allah the Exalted affirmed after the exception in His saying:

> شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ أَنَّهُۥ لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ

Allah bears witness that there is no god but He.

He said "but He," and did not say "but Allah," nor "but other than Allah"; rather He said "He." Likewise Imam al-Muizz (ع) pointed to it in his book known as Tawil al-Sharia, saying that it is "He" only. For this expression, though borrowed, is, from the minds, an affirmation of that which is outside them, without attribute or plurality.

This, whereas the treading of the path of affirming Him, the Exalted, by the use of the particle لا in the negation of every kind of the existents, is more attaining to the intent than the bare safety from likening (تَشْبِه) and stripping (tatil), and is more fitting and worthier, in the view of the scholars and the jurists among the people of religion.

The Fifth Section of the Tenth Chapter

And his saying:

"If we say He, and no thing with Him, we have negated the thing and the no-thing, and made them both originated." From where, then, is the existence sound of what is said to be a no-thing among what falls beneath origination? And the existence of what is said to be a no-thing, it being prior to origination, and it being other than Allah, such that its negation would be sound? Nay: there is nothing but the thing, and the thing that is the willed-thing (al-mashi); and the willed-thing is that which we have negated to be existent, in that there is, in the languages, that which expresses it, because of the greatness of His affair, the Exalted, and the shortfall of the composed, originated letters from signifying in a manner befitting His majesty, the Exalted.

The thing that is the willed-thing is other than Allah, who brought it into being, not from a thing, it having an entity and a right in existence upon all its divisions. Then the no-thing is a negation of the very entity of the thing, which is pure origination, according to what discourse has already passed upon. And if the no-thing is the negation of the very entity of origination, which is the very entity of existence and the true existence, how does it come to be, in existence, an originator? Those sayings are not sound.

The Sixth Section of the Tenth Chapter

And his saying:

"We have negated every form, simple and composite, from His identity, and we have made everything upon which speech falls, or upon which speech does not fall, an originated effect in truth."

We say:

How does that upon which speech does not fall, the speech from which all the existents came to be, become, all of it, an originated effect? That is an error.

The Seventh Section of the Tenth Chapter

And his saying:

"The no-thing is after the thing, since the coming-to-be of its name came to be from it at the appearing of a thing."

The no-thing is not a name that falls upon an entity having a share in existence. For "the thing" is a name, and the لا, which is the particle of negation, has negated it; and the negation of the name does not become a name for other than that of which the name was a name, nor is report made by it of other than what the sages mentioned: that folded within it is the affirmation of that which has no name. Discourse has already passed upon that which contains the answer to it, and in it is sufficiency.

The Eighth Section of the Tenth Chapter

The author of al-Mahsul said:

In the chapter of the first Creator: that the Maker, the Exalted, originated the world at a single stroke; that is, He originated the intellect as a single whole, and there emerged within it, by His determining, the forms of the two worlds and what is in them, without those forms being pointed to by their identities before the intellect. Rather the intellect's knowledge falls upon them, and they are, with it, known. Yet the intellect has preceded them in act; so, whether in act or in potency, it and the forms are all together.

We say:

This knowledge, which is the intellect that he mentioned as originated, within which emerged the forms of the two worlds and what is in them, cannot be the first intellect existent from Allah the Exalted, first of all. For that which is prior in existence is independent of conceiving that by which it exists, since its existence is bound to its Originator who brought it into being. It is not incumbent upon it to know more than its knowledge of its own essence, and that it is originated, and that its existence is not by its own essence but by another, which is its Originator, and that it is a cause for the existence of what is below it. It is like the imam, who is not obliged to know others below him, and knows no more than his knowledge that he is the cause of deliverance for those below him, and a mediator between the one above him and the one below him. Rather it is incumbent upon him to know the one above him, and incumbent upon others to know him, and to know others whose existence and rank preceded him, that they may be delivered thereby. For this reason posteriority in existence obliges the posterior to conceive all that preceded it in existence among the limits, that this may earn it subsistence and complete existence.
